solution:
Given, \(\int\limits_{2}^{3} 7^{x}\ dx = \int\limits_{a}^{b} f(x)\ dx\)
\(f(x) = 7^{x}\), \(a = 2\) ; \(b = 3\)
\(\Rightarrow f(a + rh) = f(2 + rh)\)
\(= 7^{2 + rh}\)
\(= 7^{2} \cdot 7^{rh}\)
and \(h = \dfrac{b - a}{n}\), \(h = \dfrac{3 - 2}{n}\), \(\therefore nh = 1\)
We know \(\int\limits_{a}^{b} f(x)\ dx = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} h \cdot f(a + rh)\)
\(\therefore \int\limits_{2}^{3} 7^{x}\ dx = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} h \cdot \left( 7^{2} \cdot 7^{r \cdot h} \right)\)
\(= \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} 7^{2} \cdot \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} h \cdot 7^{r \cdot h}\)
\(= \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} 7^{2} \cdot h \cdot \left[ 7^{h} + 7^{2h} + 7^{3h} + 7^{4h} + \ldots + 7^{nh} \right]\)
The bracket is a G.P. with first term \(7^{h}\) and common ratio \(7^{h}\).
\(= \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} 7^{2} \cdot h \cdot \left( \dfrac{7^{h} \left[ (7^{h})^{n} - 1 \right]}{7^{h} - 1} \right) = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} 7^{2} \cdot \left( \dfrac{7^{h} \left( 7^{nh} - 1 \right)}{\dfrac{7^{h} - 1}{h}} \right)\)
As \(n \to \infty\), \(h \to 0\), and \(nh = 1\), and \(\lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{7^{h} - 1}{h} = \log 7\)
\(= \lim\limits_{h \to 0} 7^{2} \cdot \left( \dfrac{7^{h} \left( 7^{(1)} - 1 \right)}{\dfrac{7^{h} - 1}{h}} \right)\)
\(= \dfrac{7^{2} \cdot 7^{0} \cdot (7 - 1)}{\log 7} = \dfrac{(49)(1)(6)}{\log 7} = \dfrac{294}{\log 7}\)
\(\therefore \int\limits_{2}^{3} 7^{x}\ dx = \dfrac{294}{\log 7}\)

\(\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin x\ dx = \int\limits_{a}^{b} f(x)\ dx\)
\(f(x) = \sin x\), \(a = 0\) ; \(b = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
\(\Rightarrow f(a + rh) = \sin (a + rh)\)
\(= \sin (0 + rh)\)
\(= \sin rh\)
and \(h = \dfrac{b - a}{n} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0}{n}\), \(\therefore nh = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
We know \(\int\limits_{a}^{b} f(x)\ dx = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} h \cdot [\,f(a + rh)\,]\)
\(\therefore \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin x\ dx = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} h \cdot \sin rh\)
\(= \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} h \cdot \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} \sin rh\)
\(= \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} h \cdot \left[ \sin h + \sin 2h + \sin 3h + \ldots + \sin nh \right]\) . . . (I)
Consider \(\mathrm{S} = \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} \sin rh = \sin h + \sin 2h + \sin 3h + \ldots + \sin nh\)
Multiply both sides by \(2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2}\) :
\(2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \mathrm{S} = 2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \sin h + 2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \sin 2h + 2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \sin 3h + \ldots + 2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \sin nh\)
\(\because 2 \sin \mathrm{A} \cdot \sin \mathrm{B} = \cos (\mathrm{A} - \mathrm{B}) - \cos (\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B})\)
\(2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \mathrm{S} = \left( \cos \dfrac{h}{2} - \cos \dfrac{3h}{2} \right) + \left( \cos \dfrac{3h}{2} - \cos \dfrac{5h}{2} \right) + \left( \cos \dfrac{5h}{2} - \cos \dfrac{7h}{2} \right) + \ldots\)
\(\qquad \ldots + \left[ \cos \left( \dfrac{(2n - 1)h}{2} \right) - \cos \left( \dfrac{(2n + 1)h}{2} \right) \right]\)
Every middle term cancels with the next one, so only the first and the last survive :
\(2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2} \cdot \mathrm{S} = \cos \dfrac{h}{2} - \cos \left( \dfrac{(2n + 1)h}{2} \right)\)
\(= \cos \dfrac{h}{2} - \cos \left( \dfrac{2nh}{2} + \dfrac{h}{2} \right)\)
\(= \cos \dfrac{h}{2} - \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{h}{2} \right)\) \(\because nh = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
\(= \cos \dfrac{h}{2} + \sin \dfrac{h}{2}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{S} = \sum\limits_{r = 1}^{n} \sin rh = \dfrac{\cos \dfrac{h}{2} + \sin \dfrac{h}{2}}{2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2}}\)
Now from (I),
\(\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin x\ dx = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} h \cdot \left[ \dfrac{\cos \dfrac{h}{2} + \sin \dfrac{h}{2}}{2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2}} \right]\)
Since \(nh = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is fixed, \(n \to \infty \Rightarrow h \to 0\).
\(= \lim\limits_{h \to 0} \left[ \dfrac{\cos \dfrac{h}{2} + \sin \dfrac{h}{2}}{\dfrac{2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2}}{h}} \right]\)
Here \(\lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{2 \sin \dfrac{h}{2}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\sin \dfrac{h}{2}}{\dfrac{h}{2}} = 1\)
\(= \dfrac{\cos 0 + \sin 0}{1} = \dfrac{1 + 0}{1} = 1\)
\(\therefore \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin x\ dx = 1\)

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log(1 + \tan x)\,dx\) ... (i)
By property \(\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a - x)\,dx\), with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left[1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right)\right]dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left[1 + \dfrac{\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \tan x}{1 + \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot\tan x}\right]dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left[1 + \dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x}\right]dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left[\dfrac{1 + \tan x + 1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x}\right]dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left[\dfrac{2}{1 + \tan x}\right]dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\left[\log 2 - \log(1 + \tan x)\right]dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/4}(\log 2)\,dx - \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log(1 + \tan x)\,dx\)
\(I = (\log 2)\int_{0}^{\pi/4} 1\,dx - I\) ... by eq. (i)
\(I + I = (\log 2)\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}\)
\(2I = (\log 2)\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 0\right]\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{8}(\log 2)\)
Thus
\(\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log(1 + \tan x)\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{8}(\log 2)\)

[Textbook misprint: the book passes from \(\sqrt{2}\left[\dfrac{-\cos 2x}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\) to \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left[\cos\pi-\cos 0\right]\), losing the minus sign, then silently restores it on the very next line. The answer \(\sqrt{2}\) is correct.]

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-\cos 4x}\ dx\)
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sqrt{2\sin^{2}2x}\ .\ dx\)
\(\left(\because 1-\cos A = 2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\)
For \(0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) we have \(0 \leq 2x \leq \pi\), so \(\sin 2x \geq 0\) and \(\sqrt{2\sin^{2}2x} = \sqrt{2}\,\sin 2x\)
\(= \sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin 2x\ dx\)
\(= \sqrt{2}\left[\dfrac{-\cos 2x}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\)
\(= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left[\cos 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\cos 0\right]\)
\(= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left[\cos \pi-\cos 0\right]\)
\(= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-1-1) = \sqrt{2}\)
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-\cos 4x}\ dx = \sqrt{2}\)

[Textbook misprint: on removing the second bracket the book prints \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 0+3\sin 0\); the subtraction must distribute over both terms, giving \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 0-3\sin 0\). Both terms are zero, so the answer \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) is unaffected.]

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{3}x\ dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{4}\left[\cos 3x+3\cos x\right] dx\)  \(\left(\because \cos 3x = 4\cos^{3}x - 3\cos x\right)\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\sin 3x\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}+3\sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3\dfrac{\pi}{2}+3\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3(0)+3\sin (0)\right)\right]\)
The minus sign applies to both terms of the second bracket :
\(= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+3\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 0-3\sin 0\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\dfrac{1}{3}(-1)+3(1)-0-0\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[-\dfrac{1}{3}+3\right] = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\dfrac{8}{3}\right] = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{3}x\ dx = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

[Textbook misprint: the question reads \(2\tan^{2}x+5\tan x+1\), but at the substitution \(\tan x=t\) the printed working writes \(\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{2t^{2}+4t+1}\) and carries that 4 through to its answer \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\log\dfrac{3+\sqrt{2}}{3-\sqrt{2}}\), which solves a different integral. The question as printed is solved here; its value is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\log\dfrac{7+\sqrt{17}}{7-\sqrt{17}}\approx 0.3280\).]

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2\tan^{2}x+5\tan x+1}\ dx\)
(The question as printed has \(5\tan x\) in the denominator, and it is solved here exactly as printed. Note that the textbook's own printed working silently replaces the denominator by \(2t^{2}+4t+1\) at the substitution step and carries that 4 through to its final answer \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\log\dfrac{3+\sqrt{2}}{3-\sqrt{2}}\), which is the answer to a different question.)
put \(\tan x = t\)  \(\therefore \sec^{2}x\ dx = 1\ dt\)
As \(x\) varies from 0 to \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(t\) varies from 0 to 1
\(I = \int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{2t^{2}+5t+1}\ dt\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{t^{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}t+\dfrac{1}{2}}\ dt\)
Complete the square : \(t^{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}t+\dfrac{1}{2} = t^{2}+2\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)t+\dfrac{25}{16}-\dfrac{25}{16}+\dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(= \left(t+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)^{2}-\dfrac{17}{16} = \left(t+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)^{2}-\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\right)^{2}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{\left(t+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)^{2}-\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\right)^{2}}\ dt\)
\(\because \int\dfrac{1}{u^{2}-a^{2}}\ du = \dfrac{1}{2a}\log\left|\dfrac{u-a}{u+a}\right|\), here \(a = \dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\right)}\left[\log\dfrac{\left(t+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)-\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{4}}{\left(t+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)+\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{4}}\right]_{0}^{1}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\left[\log\left(\dfrac{4t+5-\sqrt{17}}{4t+5+\sqrt{17}}\right)\right]_{0}^{1}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\left[\log\left(\dfrac{4(1)+5-\sqrt{17}}{4(1)+5+\sqrt{17}}\right)-\log\left(\dfrac{4(0)+5-\sqrt{17}}{4(0)+5+\sqrt{17}}\right)\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\left[\log\left(\dfrac{9-\sqrt{17}}{9+\sqrt{17}}\right)-\log\left(\dfrac{5-\sqrt{17}}{5+\sqrt{17}}\right)\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\log\left[\left(\dfrac{9-\sqrt{17}}{9+\sqrt{17}}\right)\times\left(\dfrac{5+\sqrt{17}}{5-\sqrt{17}}\right)\right]\)
Now \(\left(9-\sqrt{17}\right)\left(5+\sqrt{17}\right) = 45+9\sqrt{17}-5\sqrt{17}-17 = 28+4\sqrt{17} = 4\left(7+\sqrt{17}\right)\)
and \(\left(9+\sqrt{17}\right)\left(5-\sqrt{17}\right) = 45-9\sqrt{17}+5\sqrt{17}-17 = 28-4\sqrt{17} = 4\left(7-\sqrt{17}\right)\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\log\left[\dfrac{7+\sqrt{17}}{7-\sqrt{17}}\right]\)
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2\tan^{2}x+5\tan x+1}\ dx = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\log\left(\dfrac{7+\sqrt{17}}{7-\sqrt{17}}\right) \approx 0.3280\)

[Textbook misprint: on cancelling the common factor the book prints \(\int\left[1-\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right]dx\), dropping the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) that comes from the denominator \(2\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\left[\ldots\right]\), then silently restores it two lines later. The closing line also prints the integrand as \(\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{1+\cos x+\sin x}\) where the question and the working both have \(\cos x\). The answer \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\log\sqrt{2}\) is correct.]

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\cos x+\sin x}\ dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{2\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\cdot\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}\ dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]}{2\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]}\ dx\)
The factor 2 in the denominator must be carried out of the integral :
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left[\dfrac{\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}\right] dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left[1-\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] dx\)
\(\because \int\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) dx = 2\log\left(\sec\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x-2\log\left(\sec\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\log\left(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)-\left(0-2\log\sec 0\right)\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\log\sqrt{2}-0+2(0)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\log\sqrt{2}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{4}-\log\sqrt{2}\)
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\cos x+\sin x}\ dx = \dfrac{\pi}{4}-\log\sqrt{2}\)

[Textbook misprint: the book prints \(2\left(\dfrac{9}{5}-\dfrac{9}{10}+\dfrac{5}{2}\right)=2\left(\dfrac{18-9+25}{5}\right)\); the common denominator of those fractions is 10, not 5, so it is \(2\left(\dfrac{18-9+25}{10}\right)=2\left(\dfrac{34}{10}\right)\). As printed that step equals \(\dfrac{68}{5}\), not the \(\dfrac{34}{5}\) it concludes with. The answer \(\dfrac{34}{5}\) is correct.]

Let \(I = \int_{-1}^{1}\left|\,5x-3\,\right|\ dx\)
\(\left|\,5x-3\,\right| = -(5x-3)\) for \((5x-3)<0\) i.e. \(x<\dfrac{3}{5}\)
\(= (5x-3)\) for \((5x-3)>0\) i.e. \(x>\dfrac{3}{5}\)
\(= \int_{-1}^{3/5}\left|\,5x-3\,\right|\ dx+\int_{3/5}^{1}\left|\,5x-3\,\right|\ dx\)
\(= \int_{-1}^{3/5}-(5x-3)\ dx+\int_{3/5}^{1}(5x-3)\ dx\)
\(= \left[-\left(5\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}-3x\right)\right]_{-1}^{3/5}+\left[\left(5\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}-3x\right)\right]_{3/5}^{1}\)
\(= \left[3x-\dfrac{5}{2}x^{2}\right]_{-1}^{3/5}+\left[\dfrac{5}{2}x^{2}-3x\right]_{3/5}^{1}\)
\(= \left[\left(3\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)-\dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{2}\right)-\left(3(-1)-\dfrac{5}{2}(-1)^{2}\right)\right]+\left[\left(\dfrac{5}{2}(1)^{2}-3(1)\right)-\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{2}-3\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\right)\right]\)
\(= \left[\left(\dfrac{9}{5}-\dfrac{9}{10}\right)-\left(-3-\dfrac{5}{2}\right)\right]+\left[\left(\dfrac{5}{2}-3\right)-\left(\dfrac{9}{10}-\dfrac{9}{5}\right)\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{9}{5}-\dfrac{9}{10}+3+\dfrac{5}{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}-3-\dfrac{9}{10}+\dfrac{9}{5}\)
\(= 2\left(\dfrac{9}{5}-\dfrac{9}{10}+\dfrac{5}{2}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{18-9+25}{10}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{34}{10}\right) = \dfrac{34}{5}\)
\(\therefore \int_{-1}^{1}\left|\,5x-3\,\right|\ dx = \dfrac{34}{5}\)

[Textbook misprint: the last step prints \(I=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}-0\right]=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). The upper limit is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so the bracket is \(\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}-0\right]\); as printed the line evaluates to \(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\) and contradicts its own conclusion. The answer \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) is correct.]

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan x}}\ dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left[\dfrac{1}{1+\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}}}\right] dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}}{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}+\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}\ dx\)  ... (i)
By property \(\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\ dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)\ dx\)
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}}{\sqrt[3]{\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}+\sqrt[3]{\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}}\ dx\)
\(= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}{\sqrt[3]{\sin x}+\sqrt[3]{\cos x}}\ dx\)  ... (ii)
adding (i) and (ii)
\(I+I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}}{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}+\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}\ dx+\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}{\sqrt[3]{\sin x}+\sqrt[3]{\cos x}}\ dx\)
\(2I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}+\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}{\sqrt[3]{\cos x}+\sqrt[3]{\sin x}}\ dx\)
\(2I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}1\ dx\)
\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}-0\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan x}}\ dx = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
with the help of the above solved/ illustrative example verify whether the following examples evaluates their definite integrate to be equal to / as \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{1+\cot^{3}x}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec x}{\sec x+\operatorname{cosec} x}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin^{4}x}{\sin^{4}x+\cos^{4}x}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}^{\frac{5}{2}}x}{\operatorname{cosec}^{\frac{5}{2}}x+\sec^{\frac{5}{2}}x}\ dx\)

[Textbook misprint: the denominator is printed three ways. The question and line (i) print \(x^{2}+(1-x)^{2}\); the adding step and the closing line print \(x^{2}+(1+x)^{2}\); the lines the working actually uses print \(x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}\). Only \(x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}\) pairs with the numerator \((11-x)^{2}\) under \(f(a+b-x)\) and matches the generalisation printed below it, so the example is solved with that. The answer \(\dfrac{5}{2}\) is correct.]

The denominator is printed three different ways in the textbook. Only \(x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}\) pairs with the numerator \((11-x)^{2}\) under the property, it is the form the book's own working actually uses, and it is the form the "Note that" generalisation printed below confirms. The example is therefore solved with \(x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}\).
Let \(I = \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{(11-x)^{2}}{x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}}\ dx\)  ... (i)
By property \(\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\ dx = \int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)\ dx\), here \(a+b = 3+8 = 11\)
\(I = \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{\left[11-(8+3-x)\right]^{2}}{\left[8+3-x\right]^{2}+\left[11-(8+3-x)\right]^{2}}\ dx = \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{\left[11-(11-x)\right]^{2}}{(11-x)^{2}+\left[11-(11-x)\right]^{2}}\ dx\)
\(= \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{x^{2}}{(11-x)^{2}+x^{2}}\ dx\)  ... (ii)
adding (i) and (ii)
\(I+I = \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{(11-x)^{2}}{x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}}\ dx+\int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{x^{2}}{(11-x)^{2}+x^{2}}\ dx\)
\(2I = \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{(11-x)^{2}+x^{2}}{x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}}\ dx\)
\(2I = \int_{3}^{8}1\ dx\)
\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x\right]_{3}^{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[8-3\right] = \dfrac{5}{2}\)
\(\therefore \int_{3}^{8}\dfrac{(11-x)^{2}}{x^{2}+(11-x)^{2}}\ dx = \dfrac{5}{2}\)
(Read literally, with \(x^{2}+(1-x)^{2}\) as the denominator, the property does not apply at all and the integral works out to \(\dfrac{5}{2}-\dfrac{21}{4}\log\dfrac{113}{13}+110\left(\tan^{-1}15-\tan^{-1}5\right) \approx 5.5382\), which is clearly not the exercise intended here.)
Note that : In general \(\int_{a}^{b}\dfrac{f(x)}{f(x)+f(a+b-x)}\ dx = \dfrac{1}{2}(b-a)\)
verify the generalisation for the following examples :
\(\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{3-x}+\sqrt{x}}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{2}^{7}\dfrac{x^{3}}{(9-x)^{3}+x^{3}}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{4}^{9}\dfrac{x^{\frac{1}{4}}}{(13-x)^{\frac{1}{4}}+x^{\frac{1}{4}}}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{\cot x}}\ dx\) ;  \(\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{\operatorname{cosec} x}}\ dx\)

[Textbook misprint: the line applying \(f(a-x)\) carries a stray \(x\) after the bracket, \(\int_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)\left[\sin(\pi-x)\right]^{2}x\ dx\), which the next line silently drops. The closing line then states \(\int_{0}^{\pi}x^{2}\sin^{2}x\ dx=\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{4}\), a different integral from the question (that one equals \(\dfrac{\pi^{3}}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)). For \(\int_{0}^{\pi}x\sin^{2}x\,dx\) the answer \(\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{4}\) is correct.]

Consider, \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi}x\,\sin^{2}x\ dx\) ... (i)
By property \(\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\ dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)\ dx\), with \(a = \pi\)
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)\left[\sin(\pi-x)\right]^{2}\ dx\)
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)\sin^{2}x\ dx\)  \(\because \sin(\pi-x) = \sin x\)
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi}\pi\,\sin^{2}x\ dx-\int_{0}^{\pi}x\,\sin^{2}x\ dx\)
\(I = \pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos 2x)\cdot dx-I\) ... by (i)
\(I+I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi}(1-\cos 2x)\ dx\)
\(2I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\left[x-\sin 2x\ \dfrac{1}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi}\)
\(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left[\left(\pi-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\pi\right)-\left(0-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0\right)\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left[\pi\right]\)  \(\because \sin 0 = 0;\ \sin 2\pi = 0\)
\(= \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{4}\)
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{\pi}x\cdot\sin^{2}x\ dx = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{4}\)

[Textbook misprint: after applying \(f(\pi-x)\) the book prints \(2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi\sin x-x\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}dx\); the factor is 2, not \(2\pi\), as its own next line shows. In the substitution step it prints \(2I=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{-1}{1+t^{2}}dt\), keeping the \(-1\) after the limits have already been swapped, then drops that sign on the next line. The answer \(\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{2}\) is correct.]

Let \(I = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\,(1+\sin x)}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\)
\(= \left[\left(\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\right)+\left(\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\,\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\right)\right]\)
The function \(\dfrac{x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\) is odd function and the function \(\dfrac{x\,\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\) is even function.
\(\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\ dx = 2\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\ dx\) , if \(f(x)\) even function
\(= 0\)  , if \(f(x)\) is odd function
\(\therefore I = 0+2\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\,\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\)
\(\therefore I = 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\,\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\)  ... (i)
By property \(\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\ dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)\ dx\), with \(a = \pi\)
\(= 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{(\pi-x)\,\sin(\pi-x)}{1+\left[\cos(\pi-x)\right]^{2}}\ dx\)
\(= 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{(\pi-x)\,\sin x}{1+(-\cos x)^{2}}\ dx\)
\(= 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi\,\sin x-x\,\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\)
\(= 2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx-2\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\,\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\)
\(I = 2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx-I\) ... by eq.(i)
\(I+I = 2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx\)  ... (ii)
put \(\cos x = t\)  \(\therefore -\sin x\ dx = dt\), i.e. \(\sin x\ dx = -\ dt\)
As \(x\) varies from 0 to \(\pi\), \(t\) varies from 1 to \(-1\)
\(2I = 2\pi\int_{1}^{-1}\dfrac{-1}{1+t^{2}}\ dt = 2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+t^{2}}\ dt\)  (interchanging the limits changes the sign)
\(2I = 2\pi\cdot 2\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+t^{2}}\ dt\)  \(\left(\text{where }\dfrac{1}{1+t^{2}}\text{ is even function.}\right)\)
\(I = 2\pi\left[\tan^{-1}t\right]_{0}^{1}\)
\(= 2\pi\left[\tan^{-1}(1)-\tan^{-1}(0)\right]\)
\(= 2\pi\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-0\right) = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{2}\)
\(\therefore \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\,(1+\sin x)}{1+\cos^{2}x}\ dx = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{2}\)
